query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoindentation is a technique that has been used widely to study deformation at the nanoscale in various materials. Aspects of this technique that have been reported include the effect of indenter size and geometry on nanoindentation measurements. Many studies also discussed the application of nanoindentation to investigate crack growth and fracture behavior, incipient plasticity and elastoplastic deformation mechanisms. Estimation of hardness and elastic modulus from nanoindentation was established by Oliver and Pharr. Various methods for interpreting nanoindentation data were explained by Doerner and Nix and other researchers,,. Most importantly, the advantages of nanoindentation are that the onset of plastic deformation and the regime of elastic-plastic transition can be captured in detail, and mechanisms at the nanoscale can be studied. The latter is of utmost importance in nanocrystalline materials and fine structures like the friction stir processed (FSP) TRIP-HEAs that we are currently studying. Subsequently, other DP-HEAs have been developed with excellent mechanical properties that exceed most traditional dual-phase alloys. Different from many other dual-phase systems,, the fcc phase in these DP-HEAs can easily transform to the hcp phase through the glide of partial dislocations,; consequently, the volume fraction of the two phases can progressively change during plastic deformation, resulting in a steady hardening effect with increasing strain under high stress. Therefore, studying the dynamic microstructural evolution and its effect on the deformation behavior of DP-HEAs is critical to the guidance and motivation of future research on the metastability and design of HEAs. Using molecular-dynamics simulations, Fang et al. emphasized the contribution of the fcc/hcp phase transformation, otherwise known as the transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, to the promotion of strength and plasticity in these HEAs. SFE affects the plasticity mechanism, and the mechanical performance of FCC-phase alloys [], where a high SFE (>45 mJ/m2) corresponds to a perfect dislocation slip, an intermediate SFE (15–45 mJ/m2) promotes the activation of mechanical twinning, and a low SFE (<15 mJ/m2) results in a strain-induced martensitic transformation from the FCC phase to the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase [,,,]. Both mechanical twinning and martensitic transformation can improve the tensile strength, ductility, and fatigue properties [,,,,,,,,] and are known as twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) mechanisms [,]. Thus, further improving the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs by reducing the SFE is reasonable. The microstructure has a strong correlation with the mechanical properties of metals and alloys, which are usually tuned by thermomechanical processing (TMP), such as rolling, compression, and torsion, combined with heat-treatment [,,,,,,,,,]. The influence of TMP on the resultant microstructure and the correlation between the microstructure and mechanical performance of the newly developed Co-rich HEAs have not yet been revealed. The regulation of the microstructure is a prerequisite for optimizing the mechanical performance of metals and alloys; thus, gaining a deep understanding of microstructure optimization and its influence on their mechanical properties is crucial. These will become guidelines for fabricating high-performance materials that deserve in-depth investigation. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) has focused on understanding the relationships between composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties. Early studies associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but this relationship is no longer accepted as a general rule. Recent investigations have explored the effects of thermomechanical processing, alloying additions, and phase transformations on the mechanical behavior of HEAs. The trend suggests that a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches is necessary to understand the complex interactions governing the properties of these alloys.
decision.unsolved: The origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior among HEAs remain unresolved, and a mechanistic hypothesis that explains these differences is still needed. Additionally, the role of constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance in the design of HEAs requires further investigation.
decision.lever: investigate the effect of alloying additions on phase transformations and mechanical properties
decision.why: This next step follows from the trend of research on HEAs, which has highlighted the importance of understanding the relationships between composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties. By investigating the effect of alloying additions on phase transformations and mechanical properties, researchers can gain insight into the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of HEAs and develop a mechanistic hypothesis to explain the differences in deformation and failure behavior among these alloys.
